sentences.text: There's a moment at the end of a meal where the bill arrives, and everyone at the table does the same quiet calculation. Who earns what? Who can afford what? Who ordered the steak and who ordered the soup? Nobody says any of it out loud, but everybody is doing the maths. Now imagine that calculation is unnecessary, because the moment you sat down, above your head, in numbers everyone can read, was the exact amount of money in your bank account. For about a day, people treated it like a novelty. By Thursday, nobody in the country was lying about money anymore. Not because they'd become honest, because they couldn't. This is what actually happens when the last private number in your life becomes public.

So, let's set the rules properly, because the details decide everything. Every person on Earth gets a floating number, clearly visible, showing the balance in their primary account, real-time, updated by the second. It cannot be hidden, edited, or faked. It doesn't show your salary. It doesn't show your debt. It shows what you have right now. That's the whole rule. There's no second rule. And the first thing that happens, the very first thing, is that money stops being a number you know and starts being a number you're compared by. Because here's what we don't usually admit. We already publish almost everything else about our status. Your car is public. Your house is public. Your job title is public. Your clothes, your watch, your phone, the street you live on, all of it is a signal broadcast continuously for free. Money is the one thing that stayed hidden, and it stayed hidden because it is the only number that can't be faked. A car can be leased. Clothes can be copied. The number in your account cannot lie to anyone, which brings us to the first 24 hours.

The first thing people noticed wasn't the rich people. It was how many people were living one week away from nothing. That's the detail nobody is prepared for. On paper, a street looks like 30 households of roughly similar standing, same kinds of houses, same kinds of cars. The moment the numbers appear, that street turns out to be four people with real savings, roughly 20 people with almost exactly one month of buffer, and six people living in the space between two payslips. Not poor, not struggling in a way anyone would have noticed, just one, one flat tire away from a bad month.

Then the second thing happened, and this one is worse. People started spending to protect the number, because if the number is public, the number is a performance. So you don't buy the coat to look successful. You buy the coat, and then you have to think about what the coat does to the number, and the number drops, and everyone sees it drop. You can watch it happen in real time on a Saturday afternoon. Somebody makes a purchase, the number above their head falls, and for a second, they look around to see who noticed. By evening, people had started shopping at night. That's not a joke. That's what privacy is actually for. Privacy isn't about hiding wrongdoing. It's about being allowed to be temporarily unimpressive without it becoming a public event. And by the end of day one, the strangest thing had settled over everything: relief. People who had been pretending to be poorer than they were, because they were surrounded by people doing badly and didn't want to seem like they were winning, could stop pretending. And people who had been pretending to be richer than they were could stop that too. The performance ended. The comparison began.

Here's a small thing that turns out to be enormous. "How are you?" stops working. Right now, "How are you?" is a real question that nobody answers honestly. It's a social handshake. It means, "I acknowledge you." When everyone can see the number, "How are you?" becomes a question with an answer spelled out in numerals above your head. Ask it, and you're either pretending you can't see the obvious or you're being cruel on purpose. So, people stop asking. And small talk, the entire scaffolding of how strangers become acquaintances, collapses, because small talk is mostly a machine for finding out someone's circumstances slowly enough that they can choose what to reveal. You take that choice away, and you don't get honesty. You get silence. Or worse, you get a new etiquette built entirely on not looking up. Watch a cafe at 9:00 a.m. Nobody is making eye contact with the space above anyone's head. There's a whole choreography to it. People learn to look at the number the way you learn to look at a scar. You can see it, you just don't.

Then the lies go. Not the big ones, the small ones. The "I'm fine." The "I can't make it, I'm busy." The "It's on me." The "No, really, I insist." Every one of those small lies is a currency. It's how people protect each other's dignity. A friend can't afford the trip, so they say they're busy, and everyone lets them say it, and the dignity stays intact. With the number public, that sentence is visible as a lie the instant it's spoken. The friend doesn't have to admit anything. The number already did it for them. Take the office. Right now, a colleague asks how you are, and you say, "Fine," and that's the end of it. With the number public, "fine" is a claim that can be checked. So the question stops being asked, not because people stopped caring, but because asking it now means asking about the number, and everyone has silently agreed not to do that. The result is an office where nobody asks anything and everyone can see everything, which is not the same thing as knowing each other. Or take the wedding. A friend gets married, the invitation arrives, and you do the private calculation, flight, hotel, gift, the outfit. In our world, you can decline and blame the date. In that world, declining is a statement about your number, and everybody can read it. So, people go. They spend money they don't have, and the number above their head drops all evening while they smile in the photographs.
And that's the trade nobody voted for. Nobody asked, to be honest, but honesty was the only option left.
The society got more truthful and less kind at exactly the same rate.

Now the part that matters, because you don't choose who you love based on a number, but you do choose who you borrow from, who you sit next to, who you split a bill with. And all of that was being decided quietly by a calculation nobody ever said out loud.

Now it's said out loud constantly. The dinner bill stops being a negotiation and becomes an arithmetic problem. Somebody earns four times what somebody else earns, and everyone at the table can see it, and there is no version of, "Let's just split it," that isn't now a statement. So the split stops being generous and starts being accurate, which sounds fair and feels like being weighed. Then the sorting happens, and it happens faster than anyone expected. Not by class, by number. People with similar numbers start spending time together, not out of snobbery, but because it's the only way a social life stops being a negotiation. If you can see everyone's number, the least awkward thing to do is stand near people who are roughly where you are. Within a month, you could walk into any room and see that it was sorted, not by who they were, by what they had. And here's the thing that should bother you more than it does. That sorting was already happening. We were already doing it with postcodes, with schools, with which restaurant we suggested, with which party we didn't invite someone to. The number didn't create the sorting, it just stopped us being able to pretend it was about something else.

Now the version of this that nobody is ready for, family. You can see your parents' number all the time, falling slowly and then not slowly, and they can see yours. There's a conversation every family eventually has about money, who is helping whom, what's fair, what's owed. It's usually had late and badly and with a great deal left unsaid. With the number public, that conversation is never had at all because the information is already there and nobody has to be the one to bring it up, which sounds like it spares you the awkwardness. What it actually removes is the moment when someone decides to tell you. That moment, the one where your father chooses to be honest with you, is not a transaction. It is the relationship. The number gives you the data and takes away the conversation. And over time, you will find that you would rather have had the conversation.

acts.title: ACT FOUR MARKET TURNS INSIDE OUT
acts.audio: voiceover/ACT FOUR THE MARKET TURNS INSIDE OUT.mp3

sentences.text: Money doesn't stay still, so let's talk about what happens when it moves. The first industry to break is credit. Right now, a lender has to guess whether you'll pay them back. That guess is built from your job, your history, your postcode, your credit score, proxies for a thing they can't actually see. When the balance is public, the proxy disappears. Your creditworthiness isn't estimated anymore, it's displayed. And this sounds like it should be good, cheaper loans for reliable people, no more guessing. But look at what actually happens to the person with a low number. It isn't that they get worse terms, it's that they stop being able to borrow at all, because borrowing is a bet on your future, and the number only shows your present. Someone with almost nothing today might be about to be promoted or inherit or start a business. The number doesn't care. The number says no. Then prices stop being fixed, because if a seller can see your number, a seller can price to it. This already happens in a blurry way. The same flight costs different people different amounts based on what a system guesses about them. That guess gets replaced by a fact, and the person with the large number pays more permanently for everything, because they can afford to. The person with the small number pays less until the seller decides they aren't worth serving at all. Then the second market opens, and this one nobody predicted. If everybody can see what everybody has, then everybody can see who needs what, and that creates a market for helping people, not out of kindness, but because you can price it. Small emergency lending goes mainstream. Someone's number dips dangerously on a Tuesday, and by Tuesday evening, there are four people who have noticed, and one of them has made an offer. On paper, that's efficient. Someone gets the money they need, someone else gets a return. In practice, try to imagine what it feels like to be the person whose desperation is publicly legible.

Because the number isn't just information, it's a targeting system. Every scam that exists today gets simpler. You no longer have to guess who has savings. You look. Every confidence trick, the fake investment, the romance scam, the urgent call from someone who needs help, now starts with a number you can read from across a room. And the people at the top of the number scale become the most exposed people in the country. Rich people have bodyguards. Rich people have gates and lawyers and the ability to move. What they don't have, what none of them had until now, is the ability to be anonymous in a crowd.

There's a worse version of this, and it's about who is allowed to hide. Ask yourself who benefits from privacy and who benefits from transparency, and notice that it's never the same person. The employer wants your salary visible. The bank wants your spending visible. The platform wants your preferences visible. The person with power is usually the one asking for the window. So a rule that makes everyone transparent doesn't make the world equal. It makes the world legible. And legibility has always been more useful to the person looking than to the person being looked at.

acts.title: ACT SIX WE DID THIS ALREADY
acts.audio: voiceover/ACT SIX WE DID THIS ALREADY.mp3

sentences.text: Now, let's be honest about something uncomfortable. We did this. Not the number above the head, something close enough that the difference matters. Look at what a social media feed actually is. It's a bank balance you choose to display. Not your savings, your spending. The holiday, the dinner, the car, the renovation, the concert. It's a curated financial signal broadcast continuously to everyone you've ever met. We built the performance voluntarily, and we built it with the same side effect. Because once everyone is publishing a version of their spending, everyone else is comparing to it. The number isn't in your bank account, it's in the lifestyle, and the lifestyle is public. So the honest version of this thought experiment isn't, what if money became public? It's, what if the version of money we already made public, the performance of money, became accurate instead? Because right now, the public number is a lie told in images. The bloke with the leased car and the borrowed holiday looks like he's winning. The person with the real savings and no posts looks like they're not in the game at all. That's the actual distortion. Not that we hide our money, that we're already showing it badly.

So here's the question, and it's the only one that belongs to you. If it were voluntary, if you could switch your number on permanently for everyone to see with no way to turn it off, would you? Most people say no instantly, but look at the people who would say yes. The person with a genuinely high number says yes because it's an advertisement. The person with a genuinely low number might say yes too, not because they want exposure, but because the exhaustion of hiding is worse than the exposure. The people who say no are the middle, the ones with something to lose, enough to be a target, not enough to be admired, which is, as it happens, most of us. And that tells you what privacy actually is. It's not a shield for the guilty. It's the thin layer that lets ordinary people stay ordinary in public, the ability to have a bad year without it being an announcement.

So, back to the bill. Six people, one table. In our world, everyone does the calculation and nobody says it. Somebody overpays a little, somebody underpays a little, and the gap is covered by manners. In that world, the calculation is on the wall, and manners are the first thing to go. The strange conclusion is that the number wouldn't have made us more honest with each other. It would have made us more accurate, and accuracy is not the same thing as honesty. Honesty is a choice. Accuracy is just a fact that got out.
Money was never the secret. The secret was that you were allowed to be unremarkable in public.

If you want the next one, what if every lie you ever told was visible, counted, and public, it's already on the channel. And every Friday, I take one rule that quietly runs your life and break it on purpose. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one.
